teaser.text: AppLovin Corporation runs software that helps advertisers find customers and app owners sell advertising space. To understand its business, follow one advertising dollar from the campaign that starts it to the publisher, platform, and software products that share the work.

stock.meta_description: AppLovin's weighted forecast reaches $431.04 in October 2027 and $695.52 in October 2029, hinging on campaign returns and repeat spending.
stock.opening: AppLovin's weighted forecast puts the shares at $431.04 in October 2027. It hinges on campaign returns and repeat advertiser spending rising enough to justify higher training and inference costs.
stock.closing: The full memo also covers AppLovin's business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: Where could AppLovin's shares be by October 2029?

paragraphs.text: The weighted forecast puts the shares at $431.04 in October 2027, a 54% return from today. It reaches $695.52 in October 2029, a 149% return. The bear case carries 30% probability. The base case carries 50%. The bull case carries 20%.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for AppLovin, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The bear case lowers margin to 62%. Earnings fall to $5,600 million at the second date because higher budgets produce weaker returns, web tests fail to repeat and compute costs rise. The bull case retains a 66% margin and reaches $18,550 million at the final date, requiring 40% annual earnings growth from stronger model gains and repeat retail spending.

The bull path begins at $755.02 and ends at $1,484.79. Its 20% probability reflects the demanding combination of 40% earnings growth, a 25.5x multiple and substantial buybacks. The upside is plausible if incremental advertising revenue exceeds training and inference costs, but mature evidence of repeat non-gaming spend remains limited.

blocks.heading: How much cash does AppLovin really make?

paragraphs.text: Reported operating cash flow was 3,971,094 in 2025. Stock compensation is added back because it does not leave the bank when recorded, but it remains an ownership cost. The useful question is therefore twofold: how much cash reaches the business, and how much of that cash must be spent to offset employee dilution or support the computing engine?

Adjusted EBITDA can make the business look exceptionally profitable because it removes expenses such as share-based compensation. Shares paid to employees are not an immediate cash payment, but they dilute existing owners. Free cash flow is a separate test: 2025 produced $3.95 billion, while the latest quarter produced $863.3 million. There is no regular dividend, so shareholders depend on future value and effective repurchases.

blocks.heading: What has AppLovin guided for the quarter ending September 2026?

paragraphs.text: AppLovin could reach $695.52 per share by October 2029 if model-driven earnings growth proves durable and valuation confidence holds. On August 5, 2026, management guided to $2,055 million–$2,085 million revenue for the quarter ending September 2026. It also guided to an 83.0% Adjusted EBITDA margin.

blocks.heading: What has AppLovin's last eight quarters shown?

paragraphs.text: Revenue, operating income, continuing net income and diluted earnings per share all grew strongly from the prior year. The eight-quarter sequence shows a different signal: progress from March slowed sharply. Gross margin eased from March but remained above the level of a year earlier. The business was still expanding, but its pace had become more sensitive to execution.

blocks.heading: What should AppLovin investors watch on November 4, 2026?

paragraphs.text: AppLovin will report Q3 results after the US market closes on November 4, 2026, followed by a management webinar at 5 p.m. Eastern. The quarter ended September 30, so the release should show whether the improvements running in early Q3 delivered the expected reacceleration.

The key comparison is revenue against computing expense and cash generation. Stronger sales with acceptable additional costs would support management’s investment logic. A weaker result would raise a different question: did model gains fade, or did customers increase budgets more slowly? One successful release shows progress; repeated profitable improvements would establish a dependable process.
